timeline.title: Born in Edo
timeline.text: Hokusai was born in the Katsushika district of Edo, the city we now call Tokyo. The date usually given is 31 October 1760, but it is not certain. His childhood name was Tokitarō. Accounts disagree about who his father was; he is usually described as a maker of mirrors.

timeline.title: A passion for drawing
timeline.text: Hokusai later wrote that from the age of six he loved drawing the shapes of things. He may first have been taught by his father, the mirror-maker.

timeline.title: Work in a bookshop
timeline.text: At about 12 he was sent to work in a bookshop and lending library. Some early writers thought this is where he first fell in love with illustrated books, but they marked the story as uncertain.

timeline.title: Apprentice woodcarver
timeline.text: At about 14 he was apprenticed to a woodblock carver, and stayed until about 18. Learning to cut blocks by hand later helped him guide the craftsmen who cut his own designs.

timeline.title: Into Shunshō's studio
timeline.text: He joined the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō, a leading designer of prints of kabuki actors. Most sources say he was 18; the Art Institute of Chicago says 19.

timeline.title: First prints as Shunrō
timeline.text: His teacher gave him the art name Shunrō. Under that name he published his first prints, a series of kabuki actors.

timeline.title: Illustrating books
timeline.text: By the mid-1780s he was working mostly as a book illustrator, using several names one after another. He also studied styles outside his teacher's school.

timeline.title: Poor, then a fresh start
timeline.text: An early biography tells that he was once so poor he sold calendars and red pepper in the street. A commission to paint a festival banner paid well, and he vowed to give his whole life to art. Strange dates this to about 1789; it is a traditional story, not a record.

timeline.title: Out of the Katsukawa school
timeline.text: After Shunshō died in 1793, Hokusai explored other styles and was pushed out of the Katsukawa school by the senior pupil Shunkō. Sources differ on the exact timing. His first wife had died in the early 1790s.

timeline.title: Married again
timeline.text: Hokusai remarried in 1797. In all he had two sons and three daughters from his two marriages.

timeline.title: His own master
timeline.text: He passed one of his art names to a pupil and set out as an independent artist, no longer tied to any school.

timeline.title: The name Hokusai
timeline.text: He began signing as Katsushika Hokusai and published views of Edo. Strange gives 1799 for the new name. Strange says the name means "star of the northern constellation", linked to a Buddhist deity he honored. He used at least thirty names in his life.

timeline.title: A giant Daruma
timeline.text: At a temple festival in Edo he painted a huge portrait of Daruma, the Buddhist teacher, using brushes as big as brooms. Reports say it covered about 200 square meters, but this comes from popular accounts.

timeline.title: Pictures for novels
timeline.text: He worked with the novelist Takizawa Bakin on illustrated novels such as Chinsetsu Yumiharizuki (1807-1811). The two often quarreled, and why they stopped working together is not known.

timeline.title: Teaching by book
timeline.text: Now signing as Taito, he published Quick Lessons in Simplified Drawing, his first drawing manual. The preface to the first Manga volume is dated late 1812.

timeline.title: The Hokusai Manga
timeline.text: The first volume of the Hokusai Manga appeared: loose sketches of people, animals, plants, gods and daily life. Ten volumes came out by about 1819, and fifteen in all, the last after his death. Early writers disagreed on the start date, giving 1812, 1814 or 1817.

timeline.title: The Great Daruma
timeline.text: Outside the Hongan-ji temple in Nagoya he painted another giant Daruma, reported as 18 by 10.8 meters. The painting was destroyed in 1945.

timeline.title: Known across Japan
timeline.text: He took the name Iitsu around the age of 60. This began the period when his fame spread across the country.

timeline.title: His daughter Ōi
timeline.text: His daughter Ōi married in 1824 but divorced about three years later and came home. She became his assistant and a fine painter in her own right. Her birth and death dates are not known.

timeline.title: Loss and illness
timeline.text: His second wife died in 1828. Around this time, when nearly 70, he had a stroke. Early biographers say he treated himself with an old Chinese remedy and went back to work; the exact year (1828 or 1829) is uncertain.

timeline.title: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
timeline.text: In his seventies he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, later grown to 46 prints, using the newly imported Prussian blue. Its most famous print, the Great Wave, dates to about 1831. The series made landscape prints popular in Japan.

timeline.title: One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji
timeline.text: Now calling himself Manji, "the old man mad about drawing", he published the picture book One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji. In its postscript he wrote that he would keep improving until 110.

timeline.title: Living in hiding
timeline.text: In the winter of 1834 he left Edo to live under another name in Uraga. Early biographers link this to trouble caused by a grandson, but the exact reason is uncertain. He came back in 1836.

timeline.title: Drawing through famine
timeline.text: He returned during a terrible famine, when few people could buy art. Early biographers say he traded quick drawings for small portions of rice to get by.

timeline.title: The fire
timeline.text: A fire destroyed his studio and much of his work, including drawings he had kept since youth. He found new rooms and went straight back to work.

timeline.title: To Obuse
timeline.text: At about 83 he first visited the town of Obuse, probably invited by the wealthy merchant Takai Kozan. One theory says new government rules had made work in Edo harder.

timeline.title: Ceilings for festival carts
timeline.text: On later visits in 1844 and 1845 he painted ceiling panels for two of Obuse's festival carts, with a dragon and phoenix and two great waves. They are still kept in the town.

timeline.title: Still teaching, still moving
timeline.text: He published a book on how to use color, comparing Japanese and European ways of painting. He moved house once more; he is said to have lived in 93 homes in all.

timeline.title: Five more years
timeline.text: Hokusai died in Edo on 10 May 1849, still painting in his last months. Early biographers record his last words as a wish for five or ten more years so he could become a true painter; the wording differs between accounts. He was buried at Seikyō-ji temple.

timeline.title: A wave in music
timeline.text: His prints had reached Europe in the 1800s and inspired painters such as Monet and Van Gogh. Claude Debussy's La Mer (1905) is said to be inspired by the Great Wave.

timeline.title: A museum in Obuse
timeline.text: The Hokusai-kan Museum opened in Obuse, the town of his last journeys. It keeps his paintings and the festival carts he decorated, and marked its 50th year in 2026.

timeline.title: A museum at home
timeline.text: The Sumida Hokusai Museum opened in the Tokyo district where he was born and spent most of his life.

works.title: Kabuki actor prints
works.text: His first published prints, signed Shunrō, in the style of his teacher Shunshō.

works.title: Famous Sights of the Eastern Capital
works.text: Picture books of Edo published as he took the name Hokusai, along with Eight Views of Edo.

works.title: Illustrations for Bakin's novels
works.text: Pictures for adventure novels by Takizawa Bakin, including Chinsetsu Yumiharizuki (1807-1811).

works.title: Quick Lessons in Simplified Drawing
works.text: His first drawing manual, one of several books meant to teach others to draw.

works.title: Hokusai Manga
works.text: Fifteen volumes of lively sketches of people, animals, plants, gods and everyday life. "Manga" here means loose, informal drawings, not comics.

works.title: The Great Daruma
works.text: A giant portrait of Daruma painted in public outside a Nagoya temple. It was destroyed in 1945.

works.title: A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces
works.text: A series of waterfall prints from about 1827, made around the same years as his Fuji series.

works.title: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
works.text: His landscape series of 46 prints, with Prussian blue skies and water. Fewer than ten complete sets survive.

works.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
works.text: Probably made in late 1831. Impressions are held by the Met (New York), the British Museum (London), the Art Institute of Chicago, the MFA Boston and many other museums.

works.title: One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji
works.text: Three black-and-white picture books of Mount Fuji seen in every season and setting. Volumes 1 and 2 came out in 1834 and 1835; the third is usually dated 1849.

works.title: One Hundred Poems Explained by the Nurse
works.text: His last print series, picturing famous old poems. It was never published in full.

works.title: Self-Portrait as a Fisherman
works.text: A self-portrait held by the Art Institute of Chicago, which owns nearly 600 of his works.

works.title: The Great Picture Book of Everything
works.text: 103 small drawings from the 1820s-1840s for a picture encyclopedia that was never published. The British Museum acquired them and showed them in 2021.

works.title: Festival cart ceilings in Obuse
works.text: Ceiling paintings of a dragon and phoenix and of two waves for festival carts in Obuse, made in 1844 and 1845.

works.title: Treatise on Colouring
works.text: A late handbook on color, which compares Japanese painting with Dutch oil painting and etching.

works.title: Dragon of Smoke Escaping from Mount Fuji and Tiger in the Snow
works.text: Two of the paintings he made in the last months of his life, at 88.
